mcqs.question: A hidden auto-submitting form on `evil.com` posts to `bank.com/transfer`. Why does the request succeed if the victim is logged into `bank.com`?
options: Because the browser attaches the bank.com session cookie automatically to any request sent to bank.com, regardless of which page triggered it
Because evil.com steals the session cookie value and includes it in the request explicitly
Because bank.com's server has a SQL injection vulnerability in the transfer endpoint
Because evil.com is hosted on the same server as bank.com
mcqs.explanation: Browsers attach a domain's cookies to any request sent to that domain automatically, independent of which page initiated the request — that automatic, intent-blind attachment is exactly what CSRF exploits. The attacker's page never reads or steals the cookie value directly, there's no injection vulnerability involved, and the two sites don't need to share any hosting.

mcqs.question: Why can't `evil.com` defeat a synchronizer-token CSRF defense by simply including the right token value in its forged request?
options: Because the token changes every few seconds, faster than an attacker could react
Because the token is only valid from a whitelisted set of IP addresses
Because the browser blocks any request that includes a hidden form field
Because the token lives in bank.com's own HTML, which evil.com's page cannot read due to the same-origin policy
mcqs.explanation: The same-origin policy prevents one origin's script from reading another origin's page content, so evil.com can trigger a request to bank.com but has no way to read the token value bank.com embedded in its own form. It's not about token expiry speed, IP allowlisting, or a blanket browser rule against hidden fields.

mcqs.question: In the double-submit cookie pattern, why can't an attacker on evil.com produce a request that passes the server's check?
options: Because the server rejects all requests originating from a different IP address than the login
Because double-submit cookies expire within one second of being issued
Because evil.com's page can't read bank.com's cookie value to place it in the matching header, even though the cookie itself is sent automatically
Because the browser strips all cookies from cross-site requests by default
mcqs.explanation: The cookie travels automatically with the request, but same-origin policy blocks evil.com from reading its value to construct the matching header or field the server checks against — that mismatch is what the defense relies on. IP-based rejection, sub-second expiry, and default cookie-stripping aren't how this pattern works.

mcqs.question: A site sets its session cookie with `SameSite=Lax`. Does a hidden auto-submitting cross-site form still succeed in attaching the cookie?
options: Yes, Lax only restricts cookies on same-site requests, not cross-site ones
No — Lax withholds the cookie on cross-site subrequests like a form auto-submit, though it still allows it on top-level link navigation
Yes, Lax has no effect on cookie behavior and only affects JavaScript access to cookies
No — Lax blocks the cookie on every request, identical to Strict
mcqs.explanation: Lax distinguishes top-level navigation (clicking a link, where the cookie is sent, preserving normal UX) from cross-site subrequests like an auto-submitting form or background fetch, where the cookie is withheld — which is exactly the classic CSRF pattern. It isn't a no-op, doesn't apply only to same-site requests, and isn't identical to Strict.

mcqs.question: A site has both a CSRF token on its forms and an unpatched XSS vulnerability. Does the CSRF token still protect it?
options: Yes, because CSRF tokens are stored in a location JavaScript can never access
Yes — CSRF tokens and XSS are unrelated, so the token remains fully effective
No — injected script from the XSS bug runs on the target site itself and can read the token directly out of the page, then submit it
No — but only because XSS always disables SameSite cookie enforcement
mcqs.explanation: XSS lets an attacker's script execute on the target site's own origin, where it has full access to the page's DOM including the CSRF token — same-origin policy doesn't protect against script that's already running inside that origin. The two aren't unrelated, tokens are readable by same-origin JavaScript, and XSS doesn't work by disabling SameSite.

mcqs.question: A team argues their site is safe from CSRF because every endpoint is served over HTTPS. Are they correct?
options: Yes, HTTPS encryption prevents any request forgery by design
No — HTTPS protects the request's confidentiality and integrity in transit, but a CSRF request is a genuine, correctly-encrypted request forged at the origin, not intercepted in transit
Yes, as long as HSTS is also enabled on the domain
No — HTTPS actually makes CSRF easier to execute than plain HTTP
mcqs.explanation: CSRF doesn't involve intercepting or tampering with a request in transit at all — the victim's browser sends a fully legitimate, properly encrypted request, forged only in the sense that the attacker's page triggered it without genuine user intent. HSTS doesn't change this, and HTTPS doesn't make CSRF easier or harder either way since it operates at a different layer entirely.
